title: Interpretability
tagline: Probing, the residual stream, circuits, superposition, sparse features and steering
summary: What computations happen inside a language model? This course covers probing and attribution, the residual-stream view of Transformers, circuits such as induction heads, superposition, sparse dictionary learning of features, causal interventions and steering, and the open problems of understanding large models.
overview: A language model’s weights determine everything it does, yet reading off why it produced a particular answer is an open scientific problem. Interpretability research asks what representations and algorithms a trained network has learned, and it matters both for science and for safety: a model whose internal reasoning we can inspect is a model whose failures we might detect before they cause harm. This course introduces the methods and results of the field, with emphasis on the mechanistic interpretability of Transformers.

The course begins with the goals of interpretability and its main families of methods — behavioural, attributional and mechanistic. Probing and attribution are useful but easy to over-interpret, and their pitfalls are treated carefully. The residual-stream view decomposes a Transformer into paths that write to and read from a shared space, and the logit lens reads intermediate predictions from it. Circuit analysis reverse-engineers small mechanisms such as induction heads, which implement in-context copying. Superposition explains why individual neurons are hard to interpret — networks represent more features than they have dimensions — and sparse autoencoders and transcoders recover interpretable features from large models. Causal interventions — activation patching, ablation and steering — test hypotheses by changing the computation, and a final chapter surveys open problems and the uses of interpretability for safety.

Interpretability results are easy to fool oneself with: a plausible story about a neuron or an attention head can be wrong. Insist on causal evidence — does changing the component change the behaviour as predicted? — and test every interpretation against counterexamples.
outcomes: Distinguish behavioural, attributional and mechanistic approaches, and state what a good explanation should achieve.
Train and evaluate linear probes and attribution methods, and recognise their pitfalls.
Decompose a Transformer’s computation in the residual stream, and apply the logit lens.
Reverse-engineer small circuits such as induction heads.
Explain superposition and polysemanticity with toy models.
Train sparse autoencoders and interpret the features they find.
Test hypotheses with activation patching, ablations and steering vectors.
Assess the open problems of interpretability and its uses for safety.

history.title: Linear probes
history.detail: Alain and Bengio trained linear classifiers on the hidden layers of a network to measure what information each layer makes linearly available.

history.title: Integrated gradients
history.detail: Sundararajan, Taly and Yan derived an attribution method from axioms, crediting a prediction to input features by integrating gradients along a path.

history.title: The logit lens
history.detail: A blog post by the pseudonymous researcher nostalgebraist decoded GPT-2’s intermediate layers with its output embedding, showing its predictions forming layer by layer.

history.title: A mathematical framework for Transformer circuits
history.detail: Elhage and colleagues at Anthropic analysed attention-only Transformers as sums of paths through the residual stream.

history.title: Locating and editing factual associations
history.detail: Meng and colleagues used causal tracing to locate where GPT models recall facts, and edited individual facts by changing the weights of a single MLP layer.

history.title: Induction heads
history.detail: Olsson and colleagues traced much of in-context learning to induction heads: pairs of attention heads that find an earlier occurrence of the current token and copy what followed it.

history.title: Toy models of superposition
history.detail: Elhage and colleagues showed in small networks how models store more sparse features than they have dimensions, at the cost of interference.

history.title: Indirect object identification
history.detail: Wang and colleagues reverse-engineered a circuit of 26 attention heads in GPT-2 small that completes sentences such as ‘When Mary and John went to the store, John gave a drink to …’.

history.title: Sparse autoencoders find features
history.detail: Bricken and colleagues at Anthropic, and independently Cunningham and colleagues, used sparse autoencoders to decompose activations into features far more interpretable than individual neurons.

history.title: Scaling monosemanticity
history.detail: Templeton and colleagues extracted millions of features from Claude 3 Sonnet, including abstract and safety-relevant ones, and steered the model by amplifying them.
